posts.title: Why we scrub the block with salt every evening
posts.excerpt: Every evening at 18:00, after the display counter is emptied, head butcher Mateo Varga covers our end-grain wooden chopping block in coarse salt and scrubs it clean.
posts.content:
At 18:00 every Tuesday through Friday, the street outside 14 Market Row grows quiet and our front doors are locked for the evening. Behind the counter, the chilled display trays are cleared, the day's knives are washed and hung across the magnetic rack, and the cutting room settles into silence. The final task of the day always belongs to head butcher Mateo Varga at the central end-grain timber block. It is a ritual that has remained unchanged since we opened Shio Butchers in 2009: scrubbing the heavy wooden surface with coarse dry salt.

An end-grain butcher block is not a decorative kitchen counter. It is a thick, solid working surface assembled from vertical timber grain, designed to absorb the downward blow of heavy cleavers without dulling the edge of steel blades. As forequarters of beef from Harrow Lane Farm and pork halves from Millbrook Pastures are broken down across the hours, the wood drinks in moisture and meat juices. Treating such a block with chemical detergents or flooding it with hot soapy water would ruin the timber, causing the wood fibers to swell, soften, and eventually split along the glued joints.

Coarse salt provides the ideal natural solution for preserving working timber. Every evening after closing, Mateo takes a stiff wire brush and scrapes away any loose meat fibers and surface moisture from the day's cutting. Once the timber is scraped back to bare wood, he scatters two generous handfuls of coarse salt across the surface, rubbing it firmly into the grain with a clean dry pad. The salt acts as a gentle desiccant, drawing out residual moisture deep within the wood fibers while naturally inhibiting bacterial growth overnight.

The salt remains on the wood through the dark hours while the shop rests. When our apprentices and cutters arrive at 05:30 the following morning to receive fresh carcass deliveries on the rail, the salt is swept away into a waste bin with a clean brush, revealing a dry, immaculate, and pale working surface ready for the morning breakdown. There is no lingering chemical odor, no dampness, and no artificial taint to transfer onto the fresh cuts of chuck, sirloin, or shin that will be sliced at 06:00.

Taking care of our block reflects how we approach every part of our craft at Shio Butchers. We hang our beef on the bone for 21 days in the cold room, we break carcasses by hand along natural muscle seams, and we wrap every customer parcel in breathable waxed paper tied with cotton string. These traditional methods take extra time and daily attention, but they keep our tools sound and our meat fresh. When you visit our counter tomorrow morning at 07:30, the block before you will be completely clean, dry, and ready for another day of work.
